title: Integer and floating-point arithmetic
subtitle: How a fixed number of bits represents negatives and fractions, and how the ALU adds, multiplies and divides them.

signed.title: Signed integers
signed.body: Sign–magnitude spends one bit on the sign (two zeros, awkward adders). 1's complement inverts all bits (still two zeros). 2's complement is universal: invert and add 1. There is one zero, addition works the same for signed and unsigned numbers, and an n-bit word covers −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹−1. To widen a number, copy the sign bit leftwards (sign extension).
signed.steps: Represent −5 in 8 bits. Start with +5. Invert every bit, then add 1.

addsub.title: Addition, subtraction and overflow
addsub.body: Subtraction is addition of the two’s complement: A − B = A + (¬B) + 1, so one adder does both. Overflow occurs when the true result does not fit: adding two positives gives a negative (or two negatives a positive). Hardware detects it as “carry into the sign bit ≠ carry out of the sign bit”. The carry flag is for unsigned overflow; the overflow flag is for signed.
addsub.steps: Add 100 + 50 in 8-bit two’s complement. Two positives gave a negative pattern (−106): signed overflow.

booth.title: Multiplication: shift-and-add and Booth
booth.body: Schoolbook binary multiplication adds a shifted copy of the multiplicand for each 1 in the multiplier. Booth's algorithm multiplies signed numbers directly and skips runs of 1s: it inspects pairs of multiplier bits (Q₀, Q₋₁) — 10 subtracts M, 01 adds M, 00/11 do nothing — then shifts arithmetically right. Watch 7 × (−3) with 4 bits: the answer -21 appears as 11101011.

div.title: Division
div.body: Restoring division mirrors long division: shift the remainder left bringing down the next dividend bit, subtract the divisor, and if the result is negative restore (add back) and record a 0, otherwise record a 1. Non-restoring division avoids the restore step by adding instead of subtracting in the next cycle. Either takes one step per quotient bit.
div.steps: Divide 7 (0111) by 2 (0010), 4 bits. Quotient bits by repeated subtract/restore: 0011 with remainder 1.

float.title: Floating point: IEEE 754
float.body: A floating-point number is ±1.f × 2ᵉ stored as sign | biased exponent | fraction. Single precision uses 1 + 8 + 23 bits with bias 127; double uses 1 + 11 + 52 with bias 1023. The leading 1 is implicit. Step through 5.75: it is 101.11₂ = 1.0111 × 2², the exponent stored is 2 + 127 = 129, and the hex word is 40B80000.

fparith.title: Floating-point arithmetic
fparith.body: To add: align the exponents by shifting the smaller number right, add the significands, normalise, round. To multiply: add exponents (subtract one bias), multiply significands, normalise. Division subtracts exponents. Because results are rounded, floating-point addition is not associative, and subtracting nearly equal numbers loses digits (cancellation).
